turns.prompt_text: I'm screen sharing my mac mini in Ankeny to my Mac Air in Ames, the monitor I am displaying on is a vertical monitor
turns.response_html:
Managing a vertical screen sharing session between two Macs—especially when they are in different locations—can be a bit finicky regarding resolution and aspect ratio.

Since you're using a vertical monitor on the MacBook Air side, here are a few ways to optimize that setup for the best performance and visual clarity:

1. Match the Host Resolution

The biggest hurdle with vertical displays is that the "Host" (the Mac Mini) usually defaults to a horizontal 16:9 aspect ratio. If you haven't already, you should change the display orientation on the Mac Mini to match your physical monitor:

  • On the Mac Mini (via the Screen Sharing window), go to System Settings > Displays.
  • If you have a physical monitor plugged into the Mini, set the Rotation to 90° or 270°.
  • If the Mini is "headless" (no monitor attached), it might default to a standard resolution that looks tiny or letterboxed on your vertical screen.

2. Use "High Performance" Mode

Because you are sharing between two modern Macs, make sure you are utilizing the High Performance screen sharing connection. This uses an advanced media engine to reduce latency significantly.

  • In the Screen Sharing app on your Air, look for the "High Performance" icon (it looks like a small speedometer) in the toolbar.
  • This mode supports HDR and better color depth, which is helpful if you're looking at code or fine UI details on that vertical screen.

3. Virtual Display Tools

If the Mac Mini doesn't "see" a vertical monitor and won't let you pick a 9:16 resolution, a utility like BetterDisplay is a lifesaver. You can create a "Virtual Screen" on the Mac Mini with the exact pixel dimensions of your MacBook Air's vertical setup. This ensures the image fills the screen perfectly without any blurry scaling or black bars.

4. Optimize for Latency

Since Ankeny and Ames are close but still separate networks, the connection quality is key.

  • Adaptive Quality: In the Screen Sharing "View" menu, ensure "Adaptive Quality" is checked. It will prioritize a smooth framerate over perfect resolution if the network fluctuates.
  • Full Screen Mode: Use the Screen Sharing app in a dedicated Space (Full Screen) on the Air. This prevents the macOS dock or menu bar from overlapping your remote desktop.

Are you running into any specific issues with the mouse tracking or resolution scaling on the vertical layout?

turns.prompt_text: Ok, I've installed Better Display, now what?
turns.response_html:
Now that you have BetterDisplay installed on the Mac Mini, you can create a "Dummy" display that perfectly matches your vertical monitor's dimensions. This trick "fools" macOS into rendering a portrait-oriented desktop even if there isn't a physical vertical monitor plugged into the Mini.

Here is the step-by-step to get it synced up:

1. Create the Virtual Screen

  • Click the BetterDisplay icon (the monitor shape) in your Mac Mini's menu bar.
  • Go to Settings (the gear icon) > Displays.
  • Click "Create New Virtual Screen..." at the bottom.
  • In the configuration pop-up, you can name it something like "Ames Vertical."

2. Configure for Vertical Orientation

  • Resolution: Select a resolution that matches your physical monitor in Ames. If it's a standard 1440p monitor, look for 1440 x 2560. If you don't see the exact vertical resolution, you can create a custom one in the "Custom" tab.
  • Orientation: Look for the "Rotation" or "Orientation" setting within that Virtual Screen's menu. Set it to 90° or 270° so the desktop layout is taller than it is wide.
  • Click Create Virtual Screen.

3. Set as Main Display

To make sure your apps and windows actually open on this new virtual canvas:

  • Go to System Settings > Displays on the Mac Mini.
  • Find the new "Virtual" display.
  • Click the "Use as..." dropdown and select Main Display. (Note: Your Screen Sharing window might flicker or go black for a second while it re-arranges).

4. Switch the Screen Sharing View

Now, on your MacBook Air in Ames:

  • In the Screen Sharing toolbar, you should see an icon that looks like two monitors.
  • Click it and ensure you are viewing the Virtual Screen you just created, rather than the Mini's built-in "headless" resolution or a horizontal physical monitor.
  • Set the Screen Sharing window to Full Screen (Ctrl + Cmd + F).

5. (Optional) High Performance Mode

Since you are a dev using Neovim and Fish, you'll want the lowest latency possible for that vertical text scroll:

  • In the Screen Sharing app settings on your Air, ensure "High Performance" is enabled.
  • This uses the H.265 (HEVC) hardware encoder on your Mac Mini, which handles high-resolution vertical refreshes much more smoothly than the standard protocol.

Does the resolution look crisp on your vertical monitor now, or are you getting any "letterboxing" (black bars) on the sides?

turns.prompt_text: Would this not use a lot of RAM?
turns.response_html:
It’s a valid concern, especially if you’re used to "dummy" apps that use a lot of overhead, but the short answer is no. BetterDisplay is remarkably efficient because of how it hooks into macOS.

Here is the technical breakdown of why your Mac Mini won't break a sweat:

1. Framebuffer vs. System RAM

When you create a virtual display, macOS allocates a framebuffer in the VRAM (Video RAM). Because modern Apple Silicon (M-series) uses Unified Memory Architecture (UMA), this does technically come from your main RAM pool, but the footprint is tiny.

For a vertical 1440p display (1440 × 2560) at 8-bit color depth, the raw memory required for a single frame is roughly:

$$\text{Memory} = \text{Width} \times \text{Height} \times \text{Bytes per Pixel}$$

$$1440 \times 2560 \times 4 \approx 14.7 \text{ MB}$$

Even with triple buffering and some OS overhead, you’re looking at maybe 100MB to 200MB of total memory pressure. For a machine doing software engineering and game dev, that's a rounding error.

2. Kernel-Level Integration

BetterDisplay (and the underlying macOS DisplayServices it uses) operates at a very low level. It isn't "simulating" a screen by drawing pixels in a window and then recording it; it’s telling the macOS WindowServer that a new display output exists. The OS then treats it exactly like a physical monitor plugged into a Thunderbolt port.

3. The Real "Cost": CPU & GPU Encoding

The "cost" isn't actually the RAM—it's the encoding process.

  • Screen Sharing has to capture that virtual framebuffer, compress it (using H.264 or HEVC), and send it over the wire to Ames.
  • Because you are on Apple Silicon, this is handled by dedicated Media Engines (ASICs) on the chip, not your CPU cores.
  • If you were using an old Intel Mac Mini, you might see the fans spin up. On an M1/M2/M3 Mini, the impact on your build times or Neovim responsiveness will be negligible.

RAM Usage Estimates

FeatureRAM Impact (Approx.)Resource Used
BetterDisplay Background Process30–60 MBSystem RAM
Virtual 1440p Framebuffer50–100 MBUnified Memory (GPU)
Screen Sharing (High Perf)150–300 MBMedia Engine / RAM
Total Overhead~500 MB—

Pro Tip: Since you’re running a vertical setup for what I assume involves a lot of code, the biggest "drain" will actually be the WindowServer process if you have dozens of transparent terminal windows open. If things ever feel laggy, reducing transparency in System Settings > Accessibility > Display usually buys back more performance than deleting a virtual monitor ever would.

Is the Mac Mini's "Activity Monitor" showing any significant pressure, or are you just keeping an eye on it before you commit to the workflow?

turns.prompt_text: Alright I lost access to the screen, I can still see a sub-section of it but I cannot reach the menu, can I fix this from an ssh shell?
turns.response_html:
Yes, you can definitely fix this through SSH. When a virtual display or a rotation setting goes sideways and "hides" the menu bar or the interactive part of the UI, the goal is to either force the OS to reset the display topology or tell BetterDisplay to disable the virtual screen.

Since you are comfortable in the terminal, here are the best ways to regain control:

1. The "Nuke" Option: Restart WindowServer

This is the most direct way to force macOS to re-evaluate all connected displays and their positions. Running this will log you out of the GUI session and close any open apps on the Mac Mini, but it usually reverts the display layout to a "sane" default (especially if you have a physical monitor or a standard headless dongle).

sudo killall WindowServer

Note: Your Screen Sharing session will drop immediately. Wait about 10 seconds for the GUI to reload, then reconnect.

2. Control BetterDisplay via CLI

If you enabled the BetterDisplay CLI during installation, you can manage the virtual screens directly. If you didn't explicitly install the CLI tool, you can often still trigger it if the app is running using AppleScript.

Try disabling all virtual screens:

osascript -e 'tell application "BetterDisplay" to set vScreen to every virtual screen' -e 'repeat with s in vScreen' -e 'tell s to set state to off' -e 'end repeat'

If you want to just reset the resolution of the primary display:

osascript -e 'tell application "BetterDisplay" to reset resolution of primary display'

3. Clear Display Preferences (The Clean Slate)

If the OS has "remembered" a bad configuration for your Screen Sharing session, you can wipe the window layout preferences. This forces macOS to treat the "connection" as a new one.

# Remove the local display preference files
sudo rm /Library/Preferences/com.apple.windowserver.displays.plist
rm ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.windowserver.displays.plist

# Then restart the WindowServer to apply
sudo killall WindowServer

4. Proactive Fix: Install displayplacer

For the future, since you're managing this remotely between Ames and Ankeny, I highly recommend installing displayplacer via Homebrew. it allows you to describe your exact desired resolution and rotation in a single terminal command.

If you have it, you can run:

# This list command will show you the ID of your "lost" screens
displayplacer list

# Then you can force the orientation back to normal
displayplacer "id:<SCREEN_ID> res:1920x1080 hz:60 color_depth:8 enabled:true degree:0"

Which sub-section of the screen can you see?

If you can see a terminal window that is already open on the remote desktop, you might be able to drag it into the "visible" area using Option + Click on the edge of the window, or use the SSH commands above to just reset the whole environment.

Does the killall WindowServer command get you back to a login screen you can see?

If killall WindowServer didn't reset the view, it's likely because macOS is faithfully reloading the corrupted display layout from its preference files. Since you are in an SSH shell, we can strip away those preferences and force the Screen Sharing service to restart from scratch.

Try these steps in order:

1. Hard Reset of Display Preferences

This removes the configuration files that tell macOS where your monitors are positioned and what their resolutions are. Removing these forces the OS to "re-discover" the displays at default settings.

Run these three commands:

# Remove system-level display preferences
sudo rm /Library/Preferences/com.apple.windowserver.displays.plist

# Remove user-level display preferences
rm ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.windowserver.displays.plist

# Force WindowServer to restart again to generate fresh plists
sudo killall WindowServer

2. Kickstart the Screen Sharing Agent

Sometimes the issue isn't the display layout itself, but the Screen Sharing agent getting stuck on a specific "crop" of the desktop. You can force the remote management service to restart without rebooting the whole machine.

sudo /System/Library/CoreServices/RemoteManagement/ARDAgent.app/Contents/Resources/kickstart -restart -agent

3. Disable BetterDisplay via defaults

If BetterDisplay is forcing a virtual resolution that is causing the "subsection" view, you can try to disable the app's settings via the command line.

# This tells the app not to start on login, which helps if you need to reboot
defaults write pro.betterdisplay.BetterDisplay startAtLogin -bool false

# Kill the app process if it's currently running
pgrep -i "BetterDisplay" | xargs kill -9

4. The "Blind" Navigation (If you can see a tiny bit)

If you can see a small portion of the screen and have a terminal open there, you can try the Display Mirroring shortcut. This often forces all displays to sync to the lowest common denominator, bringing the menu bar back into view.

  • Press Cmd + F1 (You might need Cmd + Brightness Down on some keyboards).
  • This toggles mirroring on/off.

5. Final Resort: Reboot

If the window management system is completely hung and won't respond to killall, a graceful reboot is the safest way to clear the VRAM and the virtual framebuffer.

sudo reboot

Once you get back in: Before re-enabling the vertical virtual screen, check your Screen Sharing "View" menu on the Mac Air. Make sure "Show All Displays" is selected. Sometimes Screen Sharing "zooms in" on a single display in a multi-monitor setup, which makes it feel like you've lost the menu bar when you've actually just toggled onto a secondary virtual display.

Are you able to get a connection back after the kickstart command?

turns.prompt_text: Few of the terminal commands work: m: /Library/Preferences/com.apple.windowserver.displays.plist: No such file or directory rm: /Users/austinrognes/Library/Preferences/com.apple.windowserver.displays.plist: No such file or directory
turns.response_html:
It's likely that the display preferences have moved or are being handled differently because of how modern macOS (especially on Apple Silicon) caches these settings. On newer versions, those .plist files are often stored in a ByHost subfolder with a UUID in the filename.

Since you're in an SSH shell and those specific paths didn't exist, let's try a more targeted approach to stop BetterDisplay from forcing that layout and reset the window manager's memory.

1. Wipe the "ByHost" Display Preferences

This is where the actual hardware-to-resolution mappings usually live now.

# This will find and remove any display-related plist in the ByHost directory
rm ~/Library/Preferences/ByHost/com.apple.windowserver.displays.*.plist
sudo rm /Library/Preferences/com.apple.windowserver.plist

2. Kill BetterDisplay and its Helper

If the app is still running, it will keep "re-plugging" that virtual vertical monitor every time WindowServer restarts. Let's kill it and prevent it from auto-starting.

# Kill the app and its background controller
pkill -9 "BetterDisplay"

# Disable it from starting up so a reboot gives you a clean slate
defaults write pro.betterdisplay.BetterDisplay startAtLogin -bool false

3. The "Force Mirroring" AppleScript

Since you can see a "sub-section" of the screen, the GUI is alive but the coordinates are messed up. This script tells macOS to mirror all displays, which forces the "Main" display (with the menu bar) to sync onto whatever viewport you are currently seeing.

osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to key code 144 using command down'

(Note: Key code 144 is the 'Brightness Down' key, which toggles mirroring when combined with Command on many Mac layouts. If that doesn't work, try key code 107.)

4. Reset Screen Sharing's Local View

On your MacBook Air (not the remote shell), check the Screen Sharing app settings. Sometimes the "sub-section" issue is actually the client-side app being zoomed in.

  • Press Cmd + 0 (zero) to reset to "Actual Size."
  • Go to View > Show All Displays.

5. If all else fails: The "Discovery" Command

Since you have a degree in Software Engineering, you might prefer to see exactly what the OS thinks is connected right now. Run this to see the current display state:

system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType | grep -i "Resolution\|Rotation"

If you see a rotation that isn't "0" or "Normal," that confirms the Mac Mini still thinks it's supposed to be vertical. If the rm commands above didn't work, a sudo reboot is the only way to clear the NVRAM-cached display topology if WindowServer is being stubborn.

Did the pkill command at least make the "ghost" display disappear from your Screen Sharing window?

turns.prompt_text: rm: /Library/Preferences/com.apple.windowserver.plist: No such file or directory
turns.response_html:
It seems like the standard file paths for display preferences are being elusive, which is common on newer macOS versions where these are often cached in the ByHost directory or protected by System Integrity Protection (SIP).

Since you have SSH access, let’s try a more aggressive "reset" of the windowing environment and the BetterDisplay app without relying on those specific plist paths.

1. Locate the actual Plists

Instead of guessing the path, let's find exactly where they are hiding on your Mini:

find /Library/Preferences ~/Library/Preferences -name "*windowserver*" 2>/dev/null

If that returns paths, rm those specifically. If it returns nothing, macOS is likely storing them in a data-protected vault or solely in memory.

2. Force-Stop BetterDisplay and Clear its State

BetterDisplay might be the one re-triggering the weird layout. Let's kill it and clear its specific user defaults so it doesn't try to "help" when you restart it.

# Kill the process
pkill -9 "BetterDisplay"

# Wipe the app's internal "remembered" configurations
defaults delete pro.betterdisplay.BetterDisplay

3. Reset Screen Sharing "View" (From your Mac Air)

Before doing more on the command line, check the Screen Sharing app on your MacBook Air. Sometimes "losing the menu bar" is a client-side scaling issue:

  • Go to View > Connection Quality > Adaptive Quality (toggle this).
  • Go to View > Scale to Fit Window (make sure this is Checked).
  • If you see "Show All Displays" in the View menu, click it. You might be zoomed into only the "bottom half" of the vertical virtual display.

4. Centering a Terminal Window via AppleScript

If you have a terminal open but can't see the top bar to move it, run this script via SSH. It will grab the frontmost window and force it to the top-left corner (0,0) so you can at least use it to navigate the GUI.

osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to set position of first window of (first process whose frontmost is true) to {0, 0}'

5. Force a Resolution Change via screencapture

A weird trick to force the WindowServer to "wake up" and reconsider its bounds is to trigger a full-screen capture.

screencapture -C ~/Desktop/test.png

(This sometimes forces a refresh of the display buffer and might reveal the menu bar).

6. The "Nuclear" Reboot

If you've killed WindowServer and the BetterDisplay process and you still only see a sub-section, the virtual framebuffer is likely stuck in the kernel. A reboot will clear the Unified Memory and reset the display topology to the hardware default.

sudo reboot

Post-Reboot Plan: Once the Mini is back up, do not open BetterDisplay immediately. Connect via Screen Sharing first to ensure you have a standard 16:9 or 16:10 desktop. Once you have control, open BetterDisplay and carefully create the virtual screen again, making sure to select "Mirroring" first to see how it behaves before extending the desktop vertically.

Does the find command from Step 1 show any files, or is the directory completely empty?

turns.prompt_text: Ok, after reboot I am unable to ssh back into my mac mini
turns.response_html:
That is a stressful "silent" moment when a remote machine doesn't come back. Given that you’re working between Ames and Ankeny, there are a few likely technical hurdles that happen during a Mac reboot that can kill SSH access.

1. The FileVault Blocker (Most Likely)

If you have FileVault (disk encryption) enabled on the Mac Mini, the machine is currently sitting at a pre-boot login screen.

  • The Issue: On macOS, the network stack (including Tailscale and the SSH daemon) does not start until a user has authenticated and unlocked the disk.
  • The Symptom: The machine is powered on, but it won't respond to pings or SSH because the OS hasn't technically "booted" yet.

2. Tailscale Service Status

If you are connecting via a Tailscale IPv6 address:

  • Check your Tailscale Admin Console (on your phone or MacBook Air).
  • Does the Mac Mini show as "Online"?
  • If it shows "Offline," the service hasn't started. If it shows "Online" but you can't SSH, the firewall or SSH daemon is the bottleneck.

3. Verify Connectivity

Before assuming the OS is hung, try to see if the hardware is responding on the local network level:

# Try pinging the Tailscale IP
ping [Mini-Tailscale-IP]

# Try pinging the local IPv6 address if you're on the same mesh
ping6 [Mini-IPv6-Address]

4. How to Fix This Remotely

If it is stuck at the FileVault screen, you have a "catch-22" since you need to be there to type the password. However, there are two things to try:

  • The "Blind" Screen Share: Sometimes, the Screen Sharing app (built into macOS) can actually reach the FileVault login screen even when SSH cannot. Open the Screen Sharing app on your Air and try to connect to the Mini's IP. If it works, you'll see a basic login icon; enter your password, and the machine will finish booting.
  • Wait 5-10 Minutes: Modern Macs sometimes perform background updates during a sudo reboot (even if not explicitly told to). If it's an M-series Mac, the "High Performance" networking takes a moment to initialize.

5. If it stays dark

If it doesn't appear in Tailscale after 15 minutes and Screen Sharing won't connect, the Mac might be waiting for a physical "OK" or is stuck in a boot loop due to the display preference changes we were making.

Do you have anyone in Ankeny who can "tap" the spacebar and see if a login screen appears, or are you flying solo on this one?
